radicals.meaningMnemonic: This L-shaped radical is the <radical>lion</radical> radical, because "L" is for "Lion." It also looks like a lion's mouth being opened really, really wide. Imagine a lion opening its mouth to yawn. It looks like this radical!

This is a <radical>knife</radical>. See the sharp edge on the left and the tapered tip on top? And there's a little handle at the bottom for the... well, the handle. Be careful you don't cut yourself on this knife!
There's a <radical>ladle</radical> scooping up two drops of liquid. See the handle and the scoop part of the ladle? Imagine ladling some water into your mouth. Mmm.

First of all, there's a cross making up the middle, which automatically makes this a religion-based radical. That cross is the frame of someone's body and the things coming off of it are wings. This is an <radical>angel</radical>.
This radical looks like the fire from the burner of a stove. That's because this is the <radical>boil</radical> radical. You need to boil a bunch of water over some flames.

This radical looks like a <radical>yakuza</radical>. See him facing left, with that threatening jawline and big pompadour hairstyle? Maybe imagine a couple scars on his face too. You know, real yakuza-like.

You could also remember this because it's the evening radical under the ground radical, and people who do stuff underground in the evening (or night) are definitely yakuza.
There's a head with a little bit of hair on the top. There's also one big eye in the middle. Only one creature has a head like this, and that creature is the <radical>cyclops</radical>.

This is like one of those <radical>jet</radical>s that have little nose-wings. Imagine you're looking at the jet from the top down: this is what it would look like. It's also why this is the jet radical.

This is a tree with a drooping slide shape on top. What causes the top of plants to sag? The <radical>grain</radical>s. Imagine seeing how the heads of wheat or rice droop when they're ready for harvest. It will look like this radical. Look at all that ripe grain!

This might remind you of 米, which has three stalks sprouting upward. You can tell the difference because the top of this one is slanted from the weight of the ripe grain.
This is a very fluffy <radical>sheep</radical>. See the two horns poking up and all its wool poking out to the side? It's so fluffy that you can hardly see its tiny little legs. What a cute sheep!

You see a little drop of something on your plate. Oh no… it's <radical>BLOOD</radical>!!! Yep, you're bleeding. Now you have to wash that plate again — just as soon as the bleeding stops. Don't worry, your platelets should stop the bleeding soon. Haha, get it? PLATE-lets? Like blood platelets? Japanese blood jokes.
When a stick figure has hair that drags on the ground and gets kicked all the time, you know that hair's gotta be <radical>long</radical>. Why is it so looooong?!
You put on your hat and go outside to kick something white. It's a big white goose and you killed it with your kick. That's because you're going to cook and <radical>eat</radical> it. Yum!

This radical is just like the katakana character "ma" (マ). So let's keep things simple and make the radical <radical>mama</radical>. It even looks like a mama leaning over and gently tapping her baby to help them fall asleep.

Someone has a toe in their mouth. She's a fortune teller telling your <radical>fortune</radical>. But for her to do it, she has to take one of your toes and taste it. This better be a good fortune for you to let her put your foot in her mouth.

This is the radical for <radical>neck</radical>. Look, you can see all the vertebrae stacked up, and the little ligaments that connect it to the base of the skull! That's why this is the radical for neck.

This is the <radical>tongue</radical> radical. See that sturdy slide holding a thousand people above a mouth? An open mouth can't support that much weight, but a strong tongue can — it's the muscle of the mouth, after all.

Alternatively, you can think of this as something sticking out of a mouth with thousands of tiny taste buds on it. It's your tongue!

There's a lid on a lion. And you're stuck under the lid with the lion, which means you will surely meet your <radical>death</radical>. Or if you don't want to die, think of the poor lion. If you leave a lion under a lid for too long, death will come for it too. Either way, somebody's gonna die today.
Behind that tree the sun is rising in the <radical>east</radical>. The sun always rises in the east, so if you head that way, past the tree, you'll be going east too.

This radical is the same as the kanji. It means <radical>city</radical>.

In case you don't remember the kanji's meaning mnemonic, here's a refresher:

You see a manhole <radical>lid</radical> and a <radical>towel</radical>, both with the name of a <kanji>city</kanji> on them. Decorative manhole lids and souvenir towels — two things cities love to slap their names on, especially in Japan.

Your leader (ｲ) has become a bent spoon (匕). Well, that's quite a <radical>change</radical>. Why would your leader transform like this? Maybe they're leading a movement of people transforming into spoons, like in protest or something. And why not? If you want to change the world, start by changing yourself. Into a spoon.

Under this roof is a pig with her little ones. Your pig, because it's your <radical>house</radical>! You keep your piggies inside where it's nice and warm. They're all members of your family, so they deserve to live in your house too.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>change</radical> radical and <kanji>change</kanji> kanji are exactly the same. Except this kanji can also mean <kanji>transform</kanji>. But that's just another kind of change, isn't it?
kanji.meaningHint: Radicals be like "this isn't even my final form," then proceed to change into an identical kanji with readings and additional meanings you have to learn.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Imagine your country's leader taking this spoon and whispering some magic words to it to <kanji>change</kanji>it into a <reading>car</kanji> (か).
kanji.readingHint: Feel amazed at seeing a spoon transform into a car. Like, really imagine it, otherwise it'll be hard to remember the kanji reading later. If you feel amazed now, you'll always know that spoons changing into cars means the reading is か.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
A <radical>dirt</radical> <radical>alligator</radical> lives in the <kanji>earth</kanji>, not the water. They can swim through the earth itself! Which is pretty scary.

You can think of this word as <kanji>ground</kanji> too, because that's kind of what earth is made of.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine seeing the earth moving as a dirt alligator rises out from the ground. You should run.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The only way to keep this dirt alligator from dragging you under the <kanji>earth</kanji> and eating you is to feed it <reading>chee</reading>se (ち). That way it won't lead you to a horrific death under the earth by dragging you under and spinning you around until you eat dirt (literally).
kanji.readingHint: If you ever see someone throwing cheese on the ground, now you know why. They aren't crazy, they're saving us humans from what's lurking under the earth.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: As you dig under the <radical>ground</radical> you discover a <radical>head</radical> resting near a <radical>mountain</radical>, which are <kanji>both</kanji> strange things to find beneath the earth.
kanji.meaningHint: You'll want to focus on the part where you find both, not so much the things themselves. Think about how you can't believe you did so well finding both things at once. Usually you only find one or the other when you're searching.
kanji.readingMnemonic: But, you dig too deep and water flows into where you are. Your only hope is a <reading>row</reading> (りょう) boat floating off in the distance.
kanji.readingHint: Also think... "What's that row boat doing here?" But, it's your only hope, so you have to focus on it really hard.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>hat</radical> crowns the <radical>king</radical>, because <kanji>all</kanji> kings must have one.
kanji.meaningHint: Think of as many kings as you can think of. Guess what? Literally all of them wear hats! Think of strange hats, funny hats, normal hats, and crowns. Just make sure you're amazed by the fact they're all wearing them.
kanji.readingMnemonic: But, as you're going through <kanji>all</kanji> the kings, it turns out not all of them have hats after all. The last one you come to is hatless. He's the king of <reading>Zen</reading> (ぜん). He has simple clothes and a shaved head, unlike all the other fancy kings standing around nearby.
kanji.readingHint: To add to this story and make it more memorable, you can imagine the other kings getting upset, saying things like "All kings must wear hats! You are no king!" The king of Zen Buddhism just ignores them and begins to meditate.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>drop</radical> hits your <radical>mustache</radical>. Where did it come from? "Ah, it came from <kanji>yonder</kanji>," you say, <kanji>facing</kanji> that way.
kanji.meaningHint: Yonder is a bit of a weird word, but it fits the meaning of this kanji quite well. You'll have to trust me that it's more useful in Japanese than it is in English. When you imagine this mnemonic, make sure the drop comes from the side and hits you in the mustache with quite a bit of force. That means it came from a far distance, thus making you look over "yonder."
kanji.readingMnemonic: Who shot this drop at you from <kanji>yonder</kanji>? You look over yonder, and see a figure. It is <reading>こう</reading>いち.
kanji.readingHint:
"Who is that over yonder!" you yell.
"It is I, こういち," he yells back. "I shot at you over yonder because you weren't doing your kanji reviews often enough and you're taking up space on our database."
"But I'm paying you!"
"Oh, that's true. Well, I'm going to walk over yonder and leave you alone, then."

kanji.meaningMnemonic: With a <radical>roof</radical> over her head, a <radical>woman</radical> can <kanji>relax</kanji>. She doesn't have to worry about rain or snow or finding a place to sleep. The roof also happened to be super <kanji>cheap</kanji>, so she can even relax about her finances.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the super relaxed woman lounging under her cheap but sturdy roof. Ah, she doesn't have a care in the world!
kanji.readingMnemonic: As she <kanji>relax</kanji>es, she pulls out the <kanji>cheap</kanji>est, most relaxing food in the world: <reading>an</reading>chovies (あん).
kanji.readingHint: Think about it: anchovies cost next to nothing, they come in cans, you don't have to cook them or cut them up. You just munch them down. There's nothing more cheap and relaxing than eating anchovies under your own roof.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Think about Japan. Japan is a country made up of islands. They're basically three <radical>drop</radical> <radical>drop</radical> <radical>drop</radical>s in the large <radical>river</radical> that is the Pacific Ocean. These are Japan's <kanji>state</kanji>s or <kanji>province</kanji>s.
kanji.meaningHint: Also, another way to think of this is that the river radical is actually just three rivers, separating drops, which are capitals of various states. Rivers are usually great ways to divide up a country, and states are one way to do it!
kanji.readingMnemonic: Each <kanji>state</kanji> has its own <reading>shoe</reading> (しゅう) to represent it. The bottom of each shoe is the shape of the state, so when you step it leaves a state-shaped imprint in the ground.
kanji.readingHint: The state shoes also have things like the state birds, state flowers, and state fish printed on each of them. They're quite collectable, you should buy a pair for your favorite state!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There are <radical>mouth</radical>s, <radical>twenty</radical> of them, singing beautiful <kanji>music</kanji> together. The music seems to <kanji>bend</kanji> toward you through the air.
kanji.meaningHint: Listen to the mouths. All twenty of them. They sound great. Have them sing your favorite music. Imagine the music coming at you, bending all around in strange shapes through the air.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The twenty mouths make so much <kanji>music</kanji> that they literally <reading>cloak you</reading> (きょく) with it. They cloak you with the music.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine how you feel as they cloak you with music. Feel the music all around you, enveloping you. Become the music itself.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>narwhal</radical> and a <radical>moon</radical> are all you <kanji>have</kanji>. Imagine one of each under your arms.
kanji.meaningHint: You don't have anything else. This is it. All you have.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Everything you <kanji>have</kanji> (except the narwhal and the moon) were taken from you by a roving gang of <reading>you</reading>ths (ゆう).
kanji.readingHint: They came and took your things. Now they have all your stuff, and you only have the moon and a narwhal. You don't have much anymore, but at least you have these things still.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If the <radical>yakuza</radical> hands you a <radical>spoon</radical>, <kanji>death</kanji> is coming for you. It's the death spoon, a sign that the yakuza is coming to cause your death.
kanji.meaningHint: This spoon isn't for pudding, it's for death!
kanji.readingMnemonic: <kanji>Death</kanji> comes in the form of a <reading>shee</reading>p (し). The death sheep works for the yakuza, and kills anyone who has their spoon.
kanji.readingHint: Picture the death sheep. He looks like a black shadow, and he has a scar on his face. He's holding a bunch of spoons, from all the other people the yakuza marked for death!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>sheep</radical> radical and the <kanji>sheep</kanji> kanji are the same in looks as well in meaning.
kanji.meaningHint: You are no sheep—you study your radicals, unlike most Japanese learners. You'll learn sooo much faster!
kanji.readingMnemonic: To remember よう, we use the word "Yogurt." The <kanji>sheep</kanji> are after you. There are too many of them, and they're chasing you down, stalking you... because you stole their sheep's milk <reading>yo</reading>gurt (よう). Now you're running and crying and trying to eat the yogurt before the sheep catch up and stomp you down with their hooves.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the taste of this yogurt. You're scared and tired from running, but it tastes great!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>blood</radical> radical and <kanji>blood</kanji> are the same in looks as well as in meaning.
kanji.meaningHint: There'll be some bad blood between us if you're not studying your radicals, especially when they're the same like this kanji!
kanji.readingMnemonic:
To remember the reading けつ, we use the word "ketsup." The perfect mix of ketchup and catsup!

The radical is technically <radical>blood</radical>, but you know that radical is just a drop (of blood) on a plate. So, you ask yourself... Is that really blood on the plate? Could it be? You decide to take a gamble and lick it off. When you taste it, it's definitely not blood. No, it's <reading>ketsup</reading> (けつ).
kanji.readingHint: Feel the relief that you didn't just lick up someone's blood. Taste the ketsup taste, too. It's pretty good. Not quite ketchup, but not quite catsup. Yum!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>mouth</radical> of the <radical>king</radical> extends all the way around him (like in this kanji). Where his mouth reaches, that is his <kanji>country</kanji>, give or take a few <radical>drop</radical>s.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine his talking taking physical form. As he talks, waves extend out from him, and stop right at the border of his country before getting to the next one.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Turns out the king of this <kanji>country</kanji> loves drinking <reading>Coke</reading> (こく). Every morning that big mouth of his swallows a whole 2-liter bottle of Coke for breakfast.
kanji.readingHint: Would you drink that much soda for breakfast? Now this king says he wants to pass a law requiring everyone in the country to drink nothing but Coke! That's crazy!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Who's that <radical>woman</radical> pretending to be a <radical>jet</radical>? That's my <kanji>younger sister</kanji>. *Sigh*
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a little girl (your younger sister) running around with her arms out, pretending to be a jet, too. Prwoooooo!
kanji.readingMnemonic: Your <kanji>younger sister</kanji> is giving some <reading>mi</reading>ce (まい) a ride on her back like a jet.
kanji.readingHint: Ew, gross. Your younger sister is such a weirdo! Why does she have mice on her back while pretending to be a jet?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The only <radical>woman</radical> in this <radical>city</radical> is your <kanji>older sister</kanji>. She's the only woman surrounded by a bunch of men, but she's following her dreams in the big city.
kanji.meaningHint: You want to go to the city someday, but you're not old enough yet, like your older sister is.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Your <kanji>older sister</kanji> may have moved to the city, but she kept her pet <reading>shee</reading>p (し) with her. Now the only woman in the city is your older sister, and the only sheep is her pet.
kanji.readingHint: Picture your older sister and her sheep walking through the city. Everyone turns to stare at them, because they're the only ones of their kind.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A long time ago, someone put up a <radical>canopy</radical> over their <radical>fortune</radical> telling booth and created the first <kanji>shop</kanji>. This <kanji>store</kanji> was fortune-based, but since then lots of different stores have popped up!
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the very first store in history. A fortune teller decided enough was enough, they should be in some kind of structure where it's safe, official looking, and more permanent.
kanji.readingMnemonic: This <kanji>shop</kanji> quickly turned into <reading>ten</reading> (てん) shops! It was a good idea, after all, so all of the other people selling goods and services decided to copy it and create their own shops. The next day there were ten more.
kanji.readingHint: Picture ten shops, all made up of someone selling something under a canopy. The first one is the fortune teller, but the nine others are whatever you want them to be!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: This is the same as the radical for <radical>east</radical>, so it means <kanji>east</kanji> too.
kanji.meaningHint: Remember the radical mnemonic? The sun rises behind that tree in the east!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You see a man walk straight toward the sun rising in the <kanji>east</kanji>. It's so bright he can't see anything, so he trips and <reading>he gash</reading>es (ひがし) his knee on a rock. Yikes… But he gets back up, determined to head east, and, oh no, he gashes his other knee! OK, he should probably give up on going east.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the secondhand pain you'd feel watching him as he gashes his knee. Ow… Surely nothing in the east can be worth that much suffering?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You <radical>stop</radical> at a <radical>small</radical> <radical>slide</radical>. What were you doing before you stopped here? You were <kanji>walk</kanji>ing.
kanji.meaningHint: Question is, what made you stop? Imagine yourself walking at a nice casual pace... then imagine something that would make you stop that's incredibly interesting and strange. Maybe an alien is going down the slide? He would say "keep walking, friend."
kanji.readingMnemonic: So, you're <kanji>walk</kanji>ing around, minding your own business, when suddenly something flips up and whacks you in the face. You stepped on the head of a <reading>hoe</reading> (ほ) and it caused it to swing up from the ground and hit you.
kanji.readingHint: Of course, imagine the pain of your face. Did your nose break? After bringing yourself together, look down at what hit you. It's a hoe! How did you manage to step on just the right spot to flip it up on you like that? Examine the hoe. Pay close attention to it. Whose hoe is this? etc.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You take an <radical>arrow</radical> to the <radical>mouth</radical> because you <kanji>know</kanji> too much. You know some very sensitive information, and someone's sent a bow-slinging enforcer to pin your big blabbermouth shut with arrows.
kanji.meaningHint: Think of all the important things you know that you were hoping to blab about: JFK's real killer, the truth about Area 51, Koichi's shocking connections to the Illuminati. You better hurry and get this arrow out of your mouth so you can tell the world what you know.
kanji.readingMnemonic: One of the things you <kanji>know</kanji> too much about is the <reading>shee</reading>p (し) plan for world domination. Yes, you know that sheep are in fact plotting to overthrow humanity and take over the world.
kanji.readingHint: Take a closer look at that bow-slinging thug who fired the arrow into your mouth. Their shadowy silhouette looks awfully… woolly, doesn't it? It's undeniable: the sheep are trying to shut you up.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
The <radical>long</radical> radical and the <kanji>long</kanji> kanji are the same! 

This kanji also means <kanji>leader</kanji>, because the longer a person is, the better a leader they'll be. Or maybe it was... the longer they've been somewhere? Whatever, longness = leaderness, you know?
kanji.meaningHint: As long as you know the radical long, you know the kanji long as well.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You see a very <kanji>long</kanji> person. It's Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading> (ちょう), who has made herself long, like her street. "I made myself long so I can watch more of the street, my domain. I'm the <kanji>leader</kanji> of these streets. Watch yourself not-long person," says Mrs. Chou.
kanji.readingHint: <kanji>Long</kanji> isn't an idea that's easy to imagine in any specific sense, but you can try some other things too, as long as it gets associated with Mrs. <reading>Chou</reading>. For the most part, when you see a kanji with the radical 長 the reading will be ちょう.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
There are some <radical>horns</radical> on the <radical>ground</radical> and a <radical>moon</radical> <radical>knife</radical> in <kanji>front</kanji> of you. When you try to move, they always rotate around with you, staying right in front. You can't escape these objects, for some reason.

This kanji means <kanji>before</kanji> too. Something that's in front of you is before you, after all.
kanji.meaningHint: Perhaps it's some kind of magic, but you don't care. Why are these strange objects always in front of me? Why won't they stay put? This will get pretty freaky after a while. Try to run. Try to hide. Spin around. Do whatever you need to do. No matter what, these objects are always in front.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You're going crazy with these things in <kanji>front</kanji> of you all the time. You finally seek the help of a <reading>Zen</reading> (ぜん) master, who tells you that meditation will save you from this curse. You try it out, and sure enough, the objects are gone! It worked!
kanji.readingHint: Go ahead and do some Zen Buddhist meditation. Maybe it'll help you to remember this kanji's reading better (and calm your mind so you're ready for the next kanji!).

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You put a <radical>roof</radical> over the <radical>ground</radical> to make your own <radical>private</radical> patch of <radical>dirt</radical>. This is your <kanji>room</kanji>! That's really all a room is, you know? A covered, private place where you can have some time to yourself.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine the room you live in now. Take away all the stuff and you're left with a roof above the ground. Your own little private place atop the dirt.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The only problem with your <kanji>room</kanji> is that you can't always be alone. Because of your dad's <reading>shih tzu</reading> (しつ). The shih tzu likes to come into your room and pee everywhere. Ruining your privacy completely.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine watching the little shih tzu come into your room and lift its leg to all your things. This isn't fair. The shih tzu has its own room to pee in. Why does it have to ruin yours?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If you <radical>loiter</radical> around to <radical>poop</radical> in <radical>winter</radical> you never know what could be happening <kanji>behind</kanji> you. <kanji>After</kanji> you're done you could turn <kanji>back</kanji> to see something really crazy that you missed because you took so long to poop in the cold.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine trying to loiter while you poop in the winter. You're just trying to take your time as you squat over the snow, but soon you hear things behind you.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You finally look <kanji>behind</kanji> you and see <reading>Go</reading>dzilla (ご) and a giant <reading>こう</reading>いち having a violent battle <kanji>back</kanji> there!
kanji.readingHint: Godzilla and こういち were going at it behind you the entire time you were just lazily taking a poop in the snow?! Ahh, that's so embarrassing! And also dangerous, they could have crushed you! You should look behind you more.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: In a <radical>rice paddy</radical> you find a <radical>heart</radical> and it makes you <kanji>think</kanji>. You think a lot of <kanji>thought</kanji>s like, "Whose heart is this? Why is it in a rice paddy? Why am I thinking out loud?"
kanji.meaningHint: Think, think, think. Think about this rice paddy heart.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you are <kanji>think</kanji>ing these <kanji>thought</kanji>s, you spot someone on the edge of the rice field. He really reminds you of someone. But who? That's it! He reminds you of that bartender on The Simpsons. What's his name? You think some more. What is it? <reading>Oh! Moe</reading> (おも) is his name!
kanji.readingHint: If you don't know Moe from the Simpsons use a different Moe, perhaps the one from the Three Stooges? You should be able to come up with one. Think really hard about the Moe you know best and imagine them standing watching you from the edge of the rice field.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> that gives <radical>life</radical> is our very own <kanji>star</kanji> (which we happen to call the sun). Of course, all the other stars are probably giving life to other planets as well.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine all sorts of stars all around the universe giving life to planets as suns. These are all the stars you see in the sky and there are billions of them. I hope you don't feel overwhelmed by how minuscule we really are when you look up at all of them.
kanji.readingMnemonic: "All these life-giving <kanji>star</kanji>s need a protector," you say, pulling out your <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい). It's a big responsibility, but with your trusty saber in hand, you're sure you can defend our star system.
kanji.readingHint: Now you're soaring amongst the stars, swinging your saber at all manner of cosmic foes, and... wait. No, that was a dream. You roll over and pat your saber. The two of you are ready just in case the stars need your help.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> of <radical>tongue</radical>s is coming at you. As it washes over you, you feel each individual tongue moving around on your body, licking you. They make you feel so... <kanji>lively</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: Your entire body wakes up, you feel so lively! The tongues are making you more aware of yourself and your surroundings than you've ever been. You want to dance, you want to sing, you want to live your life.
kanji.readingMnemonic: This <kanji>lively</kanji> feeling isn't just happening to you, the tongue tsunami is licking it into all of the <reading>cats</reading> (かつ) in your neighborhood too!
kanji.readingHint: You and the cats are running around playing together, because you can't seem to get the lively feelings to stop. You have to get the energy out, but the cats have sharp claws and they're scratching you.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: A <radical>tsunami</radical> is coming, so you point your <radical>gun</radical> out the <radical>window</radical> at it. "You better turn back, <kanji>sea</kanji>, or I'll shoot!"
kanji.meaningHint: You'll have to think of the "sea" as its own entity, controlling the tsunami, otherwise you might confuse and combine the two. So when you point your gun out the window, aim it at the "sea," not the "tsunami." It's like aiming for the head of a zombie and not the arms or legs.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>sea</kanji> decides it doesn't want to die today, so it turns its tsunami around and goes the other way. You hop in your <reading>kay</reading>ak (かい) and chase after it with your gun, to make sure it actually returns to the sea and doesn't just drown someone else.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine paddling in your kayak, your gun still in one hand, as you chase the sea back to its home.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Your <radical>fortune</radical> <radical>boil</radical>s down to a single <kanji>point</kanji> in time. One point in time determines how the rest of your future will go.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine actually going somewhere to get your fortune told and watching a big boiling pot of goo. As it boils, it melts down to a single point at the very bottom. Where this point is determines your future.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you stare at the <kanji>point</kanji>, you watch in awe as it moves to the <reading>ten</reading> (てん) spot in a long series of numbers.
kanji.readingHint: Is the ten spot good? Are you going to live a long life or does this point mean you're only going to live ten more years?! Ahh!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You scoop some <radical>grain</radical>s into a <radical>ladle</radical> to do <kanji>science</kanji>. You're doing experiments on these grains in your science <kanji>course</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine carefully ladling grains into different piles so you can do science experiments on them. This course is going to make you an expert. You'll be the best in this department!
kanji.readingMnemonic: Using your <kanji>science</kanji> skills, the right temperatures and measurements, you manage to get these grains to grow into a <reading>ca</reading>r (か). This is the science <kanji>department</kanji>'s special car now!
kanji.readingHint: From your science meddling, these grains grow huge, red, and sprout sports cars when they're ripe. This is the true power of science!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: If you can steal the <radical>flowers</radical> that adorn a <radical>hat</radical> worn by an <radical>angel</radical>, you can use them to make delicious <kanji>tea</kanji>. Naturally, angels decorate their hats with only the most aromatic and delicious flowers fit for brewing.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine wrestling with an angel for its flowery hat, then running home with it. Success! Oh yes, this tea is going to taste… heavenly. *rimshot*
kanji.readingMnemonic: After brewing the <kanji>tea</kanji>, you look at the hat again and find a nametag inside that says <reading>Cha</reading>d (ちゃ). You decide that from now on this tea variety will be known as Chad tea, in honor of Chad.
kanji.readingHint: For some reason knowing the angel's name makes you feel extra guilty. Chad the angel, flowerless and hatless... Oh well. At least its name lives on in this heavenly tea.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical for <radical>eat</radical> and the kanji for <kanji>eat</kanji> are the same! Lucky you.
kanji.meaningHint: If you know the radical, you basically know the meaning(s) of this kanji. There is a second meaning added to it, though, and that is <kanji>meal</kanji>. Just think about the things you eat? What are they? In the simplest form, they are just meals. So, if you know "eat" you should be able to remember "meal" as well.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Thank goodness, you finally get to <kanji>eat</kanji> your <kanji>meal</kanji>. You're so hungry. Someone has been starving you and now they've finally given you food. Unfortunately, though, every time you take a bite, you get a <reading>shock</reading> (しょく) from somewhere.
kanji.readingHint: So, do you keep eating and keep getting shocked? Or do you not eat and continue to starve? What is worse? Obviously you're in one of the Saw movies, or something, too, so feel the fear. What will you choose? Life with shocks or death from hunger?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>neck</radical> and the kanji <kanji>neck</kanji> are exactly the same!
kanji.readingMnemonic: The only thing you do with your <kanji>neck</kanji> is use it to swallow lots of <reading>coo</reading>l <reading>bea</reading>ns (くび). Mm mm. Feel those cool, cool beans sliding down your neck. You don't really taste them, but you know they're there.
kanji.readingHint: Look at yourself in a mirror as the cool beans make their way down your neck. You can see them, like little ants marching all the way down to your tummy.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical, so it means <kanji>house</kanji>. Or <kanji>home</kanji>, since most houses are someone's home too.
kanji.meaningHint: I guess not all houses are homes, and not all homes are houses. But there's a pretty big overlap, right? And in most situations, this kanji's got you covered.
kanji.readingMnemonic: What do you do in your <kanji>house</kanji>? You <reading>ea</reading>t <reading>e</reading>ggs (いえ), that's what. You eat eggs three times a day, every day. You really love eating eggs in your <kanji>home</kanji>!
kanji.readingHint: Imagine all the eggs you've got in your house. Whole fridgefuls! It's not a normal house, but that's okay. If you couldn't eat eggs, it wouldn't feel like home.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>death</radical> and the kanji <kanji>death</kanji> are the same.
kanji.meaningHint: This thing is deceased. It ain't alive anymore.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Your <kanji>death</kanji> will be because of a <reading>bow</reading>ling (ぼう) accident. Oh, you didn't know? You're going to be hit by a giant bowling ball and crushed flat.
kanji.readingHint: You didn't want to know what would cause your death, you say? Well that's a shame. I guess you could try to avoid bowling from now on, but that won't do any good. Mark my words, your death will be bowling-related.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
Your <radical>private</radical> <radical>grain</radical>s are meant to stay <kanji>private</kanji>! You shouldn't be sharing them with the whole town, they're just for you.

This kanji also means <kanji>I</kanji>. Why? Because what's more private than you? I mean, I! Basically, some things are only the business of you (I) and those things should be private.
kanji.meaningHint: Look at your private grains. Who are those for? Why, they're for I!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You're getting into the zone, thinking about yourself (<kanji>I</kanji>) and how much you love having things that are <kanji>private</kanji> and just yours, when you realize there is a <reading>shee</reading>p (し) in this grain bag. And it's eating all of your (I's) private grains. No!
kanji.readingHint: The moral of the story is: don't let a sheep sneak into your private stash of things just for you (I). I'm sure this is a metaphor for something important...

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's an <radical>ear</radical> just sitting on a <radical>stool</radical>. Nobody's watching, so, you <kanji>take</kanji> it.
kanji.meaningHint: Feel the rush of stealing something (even though it's a weird something, admittedly). Start walking away quickly. You don't want to get caught!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You're the kind of person who likes <vocabulary>to take</vocabulary> things. "What things?" you ask. Little <reading>toe</reading>s (と). Because that isn't creepy.
kanji.readingHint: When someone asks you "Do you like to take little toes?" your answer is always "Toetally."

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
If you have <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>thousand</kanji>, you have... <vocabulary>one thousand</vocabulary>.

Simply saying 千 is the most common way to say 1,000, but sometimes you might use 一千 to emphasize or clarify the exact number.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. The only thing that's a bit weird is the reading of the 一. The ち turns into a small っ, making the reading for this word <reading>いっせん</reading>.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. When it's used as a prefix, it takes on the related meaning of <vocabulary>ex-</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>former</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word: 

You're trying to trace a person back to their origin so you can learn more about them. You finally get there - it's a castle. The problem is that it's surrounded by a huge <reading>moat</reading> (もと) and you can't get past it because the drawbridge is up. Feel the frustration of this. Think about your goal and how close you are to getting to it if it wasn't for this lousy moat.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb.

This is an intransitive verb. That means it does not take a direct object. The kanji means <kanji>cut</kanji> so this generally means that something is cut. Something breaks or snaps. No direct object here. That's why this verb means <vocabulary>to be cut</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to snap</vocabulary>. Another meaning of this verb is <vocabulary>to expire</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to run out</vocabulary>. This could be various things like your passport, or a deadline for an assignment.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. Here's a refresher to help you remember the  き portion of this word: 

Something is <vocabulary>snap</vocabulary>ping. Turns out that something is your arm. Your arm is a <reading>木</reading> (き) that grew out of you one day. "What's this ki doing here?" you ask. Then it suddenly <vocabulary>break</vocabulary>s in half! "OW OW OW! My ki! It's been cut!!"

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You have <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>writing</kanji> <kanji>letters</kanji>. What do you think these are? THAT WOULD HAVE TO BE <vocabulary>UPPERCASE LETTERS</vocabulary>, RIGHT? Whoops, sorry, caps lock was on for a moment, there.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. However, 大 uses the kun'yomi reading and 文 is an exception here, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember this:

Whenever you see an <vocabulary>uppercase letter</vocabulary>, you shout "<reading>おお</reading>, <reading>Moe</reading>!" (おおも). Your buddy Moe taught you the letters in the first place, so when you get stuck, you yell for him to come help you. And he always does. What a good guy.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You feel your <kanji>ear</kanji> getting… <kanji>hit</kanji>? This is the feeling of a <vocabulary>whisper in</vocabulary> your <vocabulary>ear</vocabulary>; perhaps a secret, or some other confidential tidbit of information. Whatever it is it has impact, which is why it feels like a hit!

Note that this word is more often used in writing than in casual speech.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji, but you know them both now, so you should be able to read this too!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You’ve already learned 仕方, which you know means "method" or "way of doing." When you don’t (that’s the がない part) have a way of doing or achieving something, you could say it can’t be helped, it’s no use, or there’s no other way. Makes sense, right? This is a popular phrase in Japanese, so we're sure you'll encounter it a lot!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: You already know how to read this from having learned 仕方, so you should be good to go!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>substitute</kanji> <kanji>task</kanji> is a <vocabulary>substitution</vocabulary>.

Note that this word has a slightly formal feel to it.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>copy</kanji>, but what is a copy? It's basically a photograph, which is why this word means <vocabulary>to be in a photograph</vocabulary>. 

In other words, this is the word you use when you point at a photo and say, "hey, I'm in this!" You know it means "to be in a photograph" because every time you appear in a photo, you're doing something <reading>ru</reading>de (る), like sticking your tongue out or giving someone the finger.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned that reading with the 写す vocab, but here's a refresher just in case:

You're going <vocabulary>to be in a photograph</vocabulary> in the newspaper. Why? Because you caused a scene by rudely beatboxing out in public: <reading>うつ</reading>うつうつ. You're probably going to appear in people's photos all over social media too. Too bad those photos won't be able to convey the phat beats you were うつうつうつing into everyone's eardrums.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The meaning of this word is pretty strange, having very little to do with the kanji meaning you learned. This word means <vocabulary>to carry something out</vocabulary>. Maybe you can think of it like someone is saying "<reading>You</reading> (う) <kanji>go</kanji> do that task!" to get yourself <vocabulary>to carry out</vocabulary> the task. Whatever you do, just know this is a weird exception word, so you may have to do some extra work to remember it.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
The reading is also a strange exception. You have to remember the おこな portion. Maybe this mnemonic will help: 

You have <vocabulary>to carry out</vocabulary> a task but don’t know how. “<reading>Oh</reading>, <reading>Cona</reading>n!” (おこな) you shout. You always shout “Oh, Conan!” when you have to carry out something tough, because it summons the spirit of Detective Conan. He’s a genius, so his spirit can help you with anything at all. Even your WaniKani reviews. Go ahead and try it now. Shout “Oh, Conan!” Did you do it? Good. Now carry out those reviews!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Writing</kanji> has <kanji>change</kanji>d our entire <vocabulary>culture</vocabulary>. In fact, when someone reads a good piece of writing it changes them, and changes their culture too. What writing has changed you so much it has changed your culture and the way you act?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 文 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

In your <vocabulary>culture</vocabulary>, everyone drives <reading>bun</reading> <reading>car</reading>s (ぶんか). Indeed, bun cars are the height of culture. And because they're made out of buns, they're much less dangerous.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Below</kanji> the <kanji>ground</kanji> is <vocabulary>underground</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>soil</kanji> of the <kanji>earth</kanji> is the portion of the earth that is made up of <vocabulary>land</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the on'yomi reading, but 土 gets modified to と for some reason. Just remember that the land you're standing on is made of <reading>toe</reading>s... millions of them. Yuck.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>diagram</kanji> of the <kanji>earth</kanji>. What could that be other than a <vocabulary>map</vocabulary>?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Don't use one hand when you can use <vocabulary>both hands</vocabulary>. This is simply <kanji>both</kanji> plus <kanji>hand</kanji> put together. It can also mean <vocabulary>both arms</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with both kanji. No problemo for a kanji master such as yourself.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Kanji doesn't go together much better than this. <kanji>Both</kanji> plus <kanji>day</kanji> equals <vocabulary>both days</vocabulary>.

This is a bit of a formal word though, you'll hear important people say it more than your friends.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 日 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

On <vocabulary>both days</vocabulary> of your vacation, you get two boats to <reading>row</reading>! <reading>Gee, two</reading> (りょうじつ) boats at once? Try not to fall in!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Here you have <kanji>both</kanji> <kanji>direction</kanji>s / <kanji>way</kanji>s. Every time you have to choose between something it's like having to choose between two ways. That's why this word is simply <vocabulary>both</vocabulary>. 

Close to the kanji is the meaning <vocabulary>both sides</vocabulary>, as well. Learn either for 両方, they're pretty similar.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This has a little hiragana attached to it but nothing that suggests it's a verb or an adjective. That means you can assume this word has the same meaning as its parent kanji.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

You wanted to remember <vocabulary>everything</vocabulary> about your trip, so you bought every <reading>souve</reading>nir (すべ) available in the entire shop to ensure you had all the mementos possible.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you put <kanji>all</kanji> your <kanji>power</kanji> into something, you're putting your <vocabulary>full effort</vocabulary> into it. Hopefully that's what you put into your kanji learning as well!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 力 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

With your <vocabulary>full effort</vocabulary>, you were able to produce a <reading>Zen</reading> <reading>lock</reading> (ぜんりょく). It's a lock imbued with the power of Zen, meaning no one and nothing could possibly break it. It's the one lock to rule them all.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know 日本 means "Japan." So, now you have the kanji for <kanji>all</kanji> added to it, making this word <vocabulary>All Japan</vocabulary> (as in "All Japan Railways" or something like that).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: You know the reading of 日本. Now just add the on'yomi reading of 全 and you should be able to read this word.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you are <kanji>all</kanji> <kanji>relax</kanji>ed you are finally <vocabulary>safe</vocabulary> and in <vocabulary>safety</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>direction</kanji> <kanji>yonder</kanji> over there is still just the <vocabulary>direction</vocabulary> of something, though a complicated way to say it, I think. This direction is the "what direction did he go in?" sort of direction.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is a single kanji with an い at the end, meaning you know it's probably an adjective. One of the meanings of 安 is <kanji>cheap</kanji>, so this is just that as an adjective, <vocabulary>cheap</vocabulary>. Time to go to a 100円 shop and get some 安い goods, ammiright?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: 

"Would you like this item for <vocabulary>cheap</vocabulary>?" 

"<reading>YAASS</reading> (やす), please!"

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When your <kanji>heart</kanji> is <kanji>relax</kanji>ed, how do you feel? What if this is after something startling happens? You would feel <vocabulary>relief</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>peace of mind</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you're <kanji>not</kanji> <kanji>relax</kanji>ed, what do you feel? <vocabulary>Uneasiness</vocabulary> is what you'd feel.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Something is <kanji>flat</kanji> and <kanji>relax</kanji>ed. That is you. What words does that describe? To me, that would be <vocabulary>peace</vocabulary>. Just imagine something that is flat and relaxed, like a field of grass with happy people in it. It's so <vocabulary>peaceful</vocabulary>!

This is the way you write the <vocabulary>Heian</vocabulary> period of Japanese history, which is probably where you'll see this word the most.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the on'yomi reading that you learned with the kanji, probably because it normally gets added on to other things, like the names of the state. Examples: カリフォルニア州, ニューヨーク州, etc.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>nine</kanji> <kanji>states</kanji>. This refers to a section of Japan from a long time ago that was presumably made up of nine states. Now it's just one big island, though, and that island is <vocabulary>Kyuushuu</vocabulary>. Go take a look at a map and find this giant island, it's a cool part of Japan!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You have your <kanji>origin</kanji> <kanji>state</kanji>. For Japan (since this is a Japanese word), that would be the main island, the big one in the middle: <vocabulary>Honshu</vocabulary>. You'll have to know some minor Japanese geography for this. Go look at a map of Japan and study it over real quick to see where I'm talking about if you don't know already.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This almost shares the meaning with the kanji. It's essentially the same thing, though when it's alone it refers to a specific <vocabulary>piece of music</vocabulary> (aka a <vocabulary>tune</vocabulary>).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji as well, so you should be able to read it.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Famous</kanji> <kanji>music</kanji> is <vocabulary>famous music</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>have</kanji>, so this verb version means <vocabulary>to have</vocabulary>. An alternative meaning is <vocabulary>to exist</vocabulary>, because having something means that it exists for you.

The kanji isn't used too often for this word, so just use the kana when you write it. But you'll see the kanji used sometimes, so it's important to be able to recognize it!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

<vocabulary>To have</vocabulary> things is very nice. You let out a satisfied "<reading>Ah</reading> (あ)…" whenever you think about all the stuff you have. <vocabulary>To exist</vocabulary> is pretty neat too, but don't think about that one too hard — we don't want that satisfied "Ah…" turning into an "AHHH" of existential dread, after all.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you <kanji>have</kanji> a <kanji>name</kanji> (that is known to people) or you <kanji>have</kanji> <kanji>famous</kanji>ness, you are probably someone who is <vocabulary>famous</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>death</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to die</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji for <kanji>death</kanji> and <kanji>body</kanji> put together make for a <vocabulary>dead body</vocabulary>. Hopefully you don't have to use or see this vocab too much.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Death</kanji> and <kanji>deceased</kanji>. That's a lot of death. This is <vocabulary>mortality</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well — <vocabulary>sheep</vocabulary>!

羊 can also mean <vocabulary>ram</vocabulary> in some contexts. After all, a ram is just a male sheep.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. When learning the kanji, you didn't learn that reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you with this word:

You see a man walk straight toward the sun rising in the <kanji>east</kanji>. It's so bright he can't see anything, so he trips and <reading>he gash</reading>es (ひがし) his knee on a rock. Yikes… But he gets back up, determined to head east, and, oh no, he gashes his other knee! OK, he should probably give up on going east.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: If you're lucky, you already know this (very) common word's reading. It's the word for "I," probably one of the first things you'd learn in Japanese. The reading for this is わたし. If you don't know that already, just think: "<reading>What, a し</reading>?" referring to the reading of the kanji, which is し.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You've seen 生活 before, right? So what about the "life" of <kanji>I</kanji>? Whose life is that? Why, that's my own <vocabulary>personal life</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>I</kanji> am the one who keeps this place <kanji>stand</kanji>ing. In other words, it's a <vocabulary>private</vocabulary> establishment — <vocabulary>privately-run</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>privately-operated</vocabulary> by ME!

私立 means "private" in the sense of a business, school, or other institution that's run by a private entity, rather than by the government or the state.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

Both 市立 (municipal) and 私立 (private) are pronounced as しりつ and it's hard to tell them apart when speaking. Although they're not official readings, people sometimes distinguish 市立 and 私立 by pronouncing them as いちりつ and わたくしりつ respectively.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>take</kanji>, so the verb version is <vocabulary>to take something</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. You already know this kun'yomi reading, so you should be able to read this word.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember 広い? Well this is like that, except a verb. When something does the action of getting wide, it means to spread out, to extend, or to stretch. You already learned 広げる, which is used when you spread SOMETHING. But 広がる is intransitive, so it doesn't take a direct object. Like: The sea spreads out before you. See? No direct object. Actually, verbs ending in okurigana that rhyme with ある tend to be intransitive like this. You can remember this because if something is ある, it's just there, existing, not acting on anything else. That's why verbs that sound like it are often intransitive too!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 広い, too, so as long as you knew that you knew this reading as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>pig</kanji>'s <kanji>meat</kanji> is called <vocabulary>pork</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>country</kanji>'s <kanji>treasure</kanji> is their <vocabulary>national treasure</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: 宝 is a <kanji>treasure</kanji>. くじ is a lottery. So if you have a treasure lottery (you win treasure if you win the lottery) then you have yourself a <vocabulary>lottery</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading uses the 宝 vocab reading, たから.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If <kanji>歩</kanji> is "walk" and you take <kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>walk</kanji>, then really you are just taking <vocabulary>one step</vocabulary>. When there's a number before 歩, it refers to the number of steps you're taking. The most common is this one, and you'll see it on urinals when they kindly ask you to please take one step forward because peeing isn't a game and somebody has to clean up after you.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is pretty standard in its trickiness. The いち shortens to an いっ and the ほ rendakus to ぽ. One step at a time, right?

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You have <kanji>three</kanji> <kanji>hundred</kanji>s. What does that come out to? <vocabulary>Three hundred</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is a little bit weird, so be careful. You should already know the on'yomi readings, but the ひゃく rendakus to びゃく. This pattern will repeat itself with 三 + many counter kanjis that can rendaku, so pay attention for it as you read Japanese.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Remember 足りる? That is "to be enough." How can you make something be enough? You keep adding things to the pile until you reach that point where there are enough! That's why this verb is <vocabulary>to add something</vocabulary>, because you keep adding things until you 足りる.

This verb is transitive, like most verbs ending in す, which is why you are adding something. It's not getting itself added all by itself. Maybe you add so much that someone tries to <reading>sue</reading> (す) you for that nasty pile of squirrels you keep outside.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 足りる, so if you know that you can add things up to this.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>car</kanji> has wheels on <kanji>both</kanji> sides, and together they make a <vocabulary>vehicle</vocabulary>.

車両 is a formal word often used in official or technical contexts. It refers not just to standard cars but also to <vocabulary>train car</vocabulary>s and other vehicles that carry people or goods. You'll commonly see it in public transportation terms, on signs like "No vehicles allowed," or in driver's license and traffic law classifications.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This is the adverb version of the kanji <kanji>early</kanji>. It's a little thing you can begin sentences with to say you're doing something <vocabulary>early</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>quickly</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since you already know the reading of the vocab word 早い, you should be able to read this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This is your older sister, by the way. Not somebody else's.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet,  so here's a mnemonic to help you remember:

Picture your <vocabulary>older sister</vocabulary> (even if you don't have one), her birthday is coming up and there's only one thing she wants from you. <reading>A ne</reading>cklace (あね). She's wanted a necklace for years and you're finally going to give her one. She'll be so happy.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You'll see this attached to other words... like "waiting" or "guest." When you see this, you'll know it is a ___ room, making this word mean <vocabulary>room</vocabulary> (same as the kanji).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the on'yomi reading. Don't type the 〜 out when writing the answer. It's just there to let you know that there's usually something attached to this word.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: <kanji>Grass</kanji> covering the <kanji>earth</kanji> is a <vocabulary>meadow</vocabulary>. Or, if you're less creative, it's <vocabulary>grassland</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is a combination of kun'yomi and on'yomi readings. That being said, both readings for both kanji are the readings you learned with the kanji so you should be able to read this.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: A <kanji>country</kanji> <kanji>king</kanji> is still a <vocabulary>king</vocabulary>, just of a bigger area.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>water</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji> is the planet <vocabulary>Mercury</vocabulary>. That's where we hid all of our secret moon water. Mercury looks enough like our moon, so we put it there so no one could find it.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>gold</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji> is <vocabulary>Venus</vocabulary>. It's the only planet in our solar system that's the same color as gold.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. Remember how 生きる means "to live?" Well this is what happens right after it starts to live. It begins <vocabulary>to grow</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

You'll know a seedling has managed <vocabulary>to grow</vocabulary> when you hear it yell "<reading>hah</reading> (は)!" in a cute little baby plant voice. "Hah! I knew I could do it! I knew I could grow! Hah!"

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The <kanji>ground</kanji> <kanji>star</kanji> is <vocabulary>Saturn</vocabulary>. That's why it's called "sat"urn. Because the first people to find it sat on the ground there. It's a star made completely of sit-on-able ground.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If you have <kanji>lively</kanji> <kanji>energy</kanji> you have more than enough <vocabulary>energy</vocabulary> for everyone to start noticing. They come up to you and compliment you on your amazing <vocabulary>liveliness</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just be careful because かつ is being shortened here to かっ. It's a pretty common change for on'yomi ending in つ, so keep your eyes open for more that do this!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If you're in the <kanji>middle</kanji> of the <kanji>ground</kanji>, then you're most likely <vocabulary>underground</vocabulary>. Are you a moleperson? That's pretty cool.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
If you make <kanji>lively</kanji> <kanji>use</kanji> of something, you're probably <vocabulary>utilizing</vocabulary> it or making <vocabulary>practical use</vocabulary> of it.

活用 means making full use of something. In the context of Japanese grammar, 活用 also refers to the <vocabulary>conjugation</vocabulary> of verbs and adjectives.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>know</kanji> so the verb version means <vocabulary>to know</vocabulary>. It can additionally refer to how one comes to know something, so it also means <vocabulary>to learn</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to find out</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading already with the kanji, so you're good to go! Yay!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Your <kanji>hand</kanji>'s <kanji>neck</kanji> is your <vocabulary>wrist</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi readings from both kanji, probably because it includes body parts. You know them both already, so now you know this too!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If you <kanji>exit</kanji> somewhere in order to go to your <kanji>company</kanji>, that's <vocabulary>going to the office</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>arriving at the office</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>coming to work</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own. Just watch out for  the しゅつ, which gets changed to しゅっ, as many つs do in this situation.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Your <kanji>origin</kanji> partner is a partner you had originally, but don't have anymore. In other words, this is your <vocabulary>ex-partner</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>former partner</vocabulary>.

Like in English, this word is fairly formal, and it covers any kind of ex-partner, including business and romantic partners.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi of 元 and then it's just kana, so you should know how to read this!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You've already learned 石, which means <kanji>stone</kanji>. You haven't seen ころ before, but it's sometimes used as a casual suffix for small, round things. Put the two together, and you've got a <vocabulary>small stone</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>pebble</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This uses the kun'yomi of 石, which you've already learned, and adds a bit of hiragana, so you should be able to read this! If you need help remembering the ころ bit, though, here's a mnemonic for you:

Even a <vocabulary>small stone</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>pebble</vocabulary> could have something amazing at its <reading>core</reading> (ころ). I mean, anything at all could be in that core! Gold, diamonds… Maybe even a chocolate filling! You'd better gather up some small stones and pebbles and start bashing them open to look at their cores. Otherwise, you could be missing out.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
Here you have <kanji>other</kanji> and <kanji>person</kanji> joined together by the particle の, which shows that "other" is describing "person". So this means <vocabulary>someone else</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>other people</vocabulary>.

This is more general than 他人, which you already learned. 他の人 can be anyone that's not the speaker, or not the person being talked about. 他人, on the other hand, has an added implication that the person is someone unknown or unrelated.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This uses the kanji's kun'yomi readings, which you've already learned. As long as you remember those, you should be good to go!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You already know that 一千 is "<kanji>one</kanji> <kanji>thousand</kanji>," and that 万 is "<kanji>ten thousand</kanji>." Add all those zeros together (or multiply 1,000 with 10,000) and you end up with <vocabulary>ten million</vocabulary>. 

You learned that 千 is the more common and default way to say 1,000 and 一千 is sometimes used for emphasis or clarity. Well, to say ten million, you almost always say it as 一千万. I mean, who wouldn't want to emphasize ten million! It's ten million, you know?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: You already learned how to read both 一千 and 万, so just put those two readings together and you're good to go!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You have <kanji>ten</kanji> <kanji>part</kanji>s out of ten. Which means you have quite <vocabulary>enough</vocabulary>. The amount you have is <vocabulary>sufficient</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>plenty</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
The <kanji>west</kanji> bit of ヨーロッパ (Europe) is <vocabulary>Western Europe</vocabulary>. 

Have you ever been to 西ヨーロッパ? You know, places like France, the UK, and Belgium, with all their wine and cheese and beer… Western Europe!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This uses the kun'yomi reading of 西, which you've already learned, so you should be good to go here!
